questions.question: If a truck collides with a small car, why does the car usually experience more damage even though both vehicles exert equal and opposite forces on each other?
questions.learning_objective: Understand Newton's Third Law and distinguish interaction force from acceleration and damage.
questions.target_misconception: The larger object exerts a greater force during a collision.
solution_steps: Identify the two interacting objects and the forces they exert on each other.
Apply Newton's Third Law: the interaction forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
Use Newton's Second Law to compare the accelerations produced by the forces on objects of different masses.
Explain why the smaller mass can experience greater acceleration.
Distinguish acceleration from damage, which also depends on structure, deformation and energy absorption.
questions.reference_answer: The forces on the truck and car are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. However, because the car has much less mass, the same force produces a greater acceleration. The damage also depends on factors such as each vehicle's structure, deformation and energy absorption; it is not determined by acceleration alone.

questions.question: A person carries a bag horizontally across a room at a constant height and speed. Is the upward supporting force exerted by the person doing mechanical work on the bag? Why or why not?
questions.learning_objective: Understand the relationship between force, displacement and mechanical work.
questions.target_misconception: Any application of force automatically means mechanical work is done on an object.
expected_concepts: Work done by a particular force
solution_steps: Identify the upward supporting force exerted on the bag.
Identify that the bag's displacement is horizontal.
Determine that the angle between the force and displacement is 90 degrees.
Apply W = Fd cos(theta).
Conclude that the supporting force does zero mechanical work on the bag in this idealized situation.
questions.reference_answer: The upward supporting force is perpendicular to the bag's horizontal displacement. Since W = Fd cos(90 degrees) = 0, that force does zero mechanical work on the bag. This does not mean the person uses no metabolic energy; it refers only to mechanical work done by the supporting force on the bag.

questions.question: Two identical bulbs are connected to the same ideal battery. They are first connected in series and then, in a separate setup, in parallel. In which setup will each bulb glow brighter, and why?
questions.learning_objective: Understand how voltage, current and resistance affect power in series and parallel circuits.
questions.target_misconception: Each bulb receives the same voltage in a series circuit, or adding parallel branches makes the voltage across each bulb smaller.
solution_steps: Recognize that identical bulbs have equal resistance.
In series, explain that the battery voltage is shared between the two identical bulbs.
In parallel, explain that each bulb is connected across the full battery voltage.
Use P = V^2/R for each bulb to compare their power, assuming an ideal battery and identical bulbs.
Conclude that each bulb is brighter in the parallel arrangement.
questions.reference_answer: Each bulb glows brighter in parallel. In series, the identical bulbs share the battery voltage, so each gets about half the voltage. In parallel, each bulb gets the full battery voltage. Since the bulbs have the same resistance and power is P = V^2/R, each bulb dissipates more power in the parallel setup.

questions.question: A person standing on a frictionless surface throws a heavy ball forward and moves backward. Why does the person move in the opposite direction even though they did not intentionally push themselves backward?
questions.learning_objective: Understand conservation of momentum in an interaction.
questions.target_misconception: The ball takes momentum away from the person, so momentum conservation does not apply to the combined system.
solution_steps: Identify the person and ball as a combined system.
Note that the system initially has zero total momentum if it is at rest.
Explain that throwing the ball forward gives it forward momentum.
Apply conservation of momentum to show that the person gains equal and opposite momentum.
Explain that the person's backward motion balances the ball's forward momentum.
questions.reference_answer: Before the throw, the person-ball system has zero total momentum. When the person throws the ball forward, the ball gains forward momentum. With no net external horizontal force on the system, total momentum is conserved, so the person gains equal and opposite backward momentum.

questions.question: A student solves x^2 = 9 and concludes that x = 3 is the only solution. Is the student correct? Explain.
questions.learning_objective: Understand solving quadratic equations and the significance of positive and negative roots.
questions.target_misconception: Taking the square root of a number only produces its positive root.
solution_steps: Interpret the equation x^2 = 9.
Ask which numbers produce 9 when squared.
Identify both 3 and -3.
Verify both solutions by substitution.
Explain why both satisfy the original equation.
questions.reference_answer: The student is incorrect. Both x = 3 and x = -3 satisfy the equation because 3^2 = 9 and (-3)^2 = 9. Therefore, the complete solution set is x = plus or minus 3.

questions.question: A fair coin is flipped five times and lands on heads every time. Is tails now more likely to occur on the sixth flip? Explain.
questions.learning_objective: Understand independent events and avoid the gambler's fallacy.
questions.target_misconception: An outcome becomes more likely because it has not occurred recently.
solution_steps: Establish that the coin is fair.
Identify the sixth flip as a separate event.
Explain that previous outcomes do not influence the next flip.
State that the probability of heads and tails is one half each.
Explain why tails is not 'due' to occur.
questions.reference_answer: No. Each flip is independent. The probability of heads and tails on the sixth flip remains 1/2, regardless of the previous five outcomes. The belief that tails is now due is the gambler's fallacy.

questions.question: An object's position is given by s(t) = t^2 metres, where t is measured in seconds. What does the derivative of s(t) tell us, and what is the object's instantaneous velocity at t = 3 seconds?
questions.learning_objective: Interpret a derivative as an instantaneous rate of change and apply basic differentiation.
questions.target_misconception: A derivative gives the total change in a quantity rather than its instantaneous rate of change.
expected_concepts: Velocity as rate of change of position
solution_steps: Recognize that velocity is the rate of change of position with respect to time.
Differentiate s(t) = t^2 to obtain ds/dt = 2t.
Substitute t = 3 seconds.
Calculate the instantaneous velocity as 6 metres per second.
Explain the derivative's meaning as the slope of the position-time graph at that instant.
questions.reference_answer: The derivative gives the instantaneous rate at which position changes, which is velocity. Differentiating s(t) = t^2 gives v(t) = 2t, so at t = 3 seconds the instantaneous velocity is 6 m/s.

questions.question: Consider the limit as x approaches 2 of (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2). Direct substitution gives 0/0. Does that mean the limit does not exist? Explain.
questions.learning_objective: Understand the meaning of an indeterminate form and evaluate a simple limit by algebraic simplification.
questions.target_misconception: Getting 0/0 after substitution proves that a limit does not exist or equals zero.
solution_steps: Substitute x = 2 and observe the indeterminate form 0/0.
Factor the numerator as (x - 2)(x + 2).
For x not equal to 2, cancel the common factor x - 2.
Evaluate the limit of the simplified expression x + 2 as x approaches 2.
Conclude that the limit is 4 even though the original expression is undefined at x = 2.
questions.reference_answer: No. The form 0/0 is indeterminate; it does not by itself tell us whether the limit exists. Factor x^2 - 4 as (x - 2)(x + 2), cancel x - 2 for nearby x values, and take the limit of x + 2. The limit is 4.

questions.question: If two non-zero vectors have a dot product of zero, what does that tell you about the angle between them? Why?
questions.learning_objective: Understand the geometric meaning of the dot product.
questions.target_misconception: A zero dot product means one of the vectors must be the zero vector.
solution_steps: Recall that a dot product can be written as a·b = |a||b| cos(theta).
Use the fact that both vectors are non-zero, so their magnitudes are non-zero.
Set the dot product to zero and infer that cos(theta) is zero.
Identify the angle as 90 degrees.
Conclude that the vectors are perpendicular.
questions.reference_answer: For non-zero vectors, a·b = |a||b| cos(theta). Since both magnitudes are non-zero and the dot product is zero, cos(theta) must be zero. Therefore, the angle is 90 degrees and the vectors are perpendicular.

questions.question: Why does atomic radius generally decrease as we move from left to right across a period, even though more electrons are being added?
questions.learning_objective: Understand the relationship between nuclear charge, shielding and atomic size across a period.
questions.target_misconception: Adding more electrons always makes an atom larger, regardless of the change in nuclear charge.
solution_steps: Recognize that electrons are added to the same principal shell across a period.
Recognize that the number of protons in the nucleus also increases.
Explain that shielding does not increase enough to cancel the increase in nuclear charge.
Connect the increased effective nuclear attraction to electrons being pulled closer.
Conclude that atomic radius generally decreases across a period.
questions.reference_answer: Across a period, protons are added to the nucleus while added electrons generally enter the same principal shell. Shielding does not increase enough to offset the increased nuclear charge, so effective nuclear attraction increases and pulls the electron cloud closer. Thus atomic radius generally decreases.

questions.question: Solid table salt does not conduct electricity well, but molten salt can conduct electricity. If salt contains charged ions in both cases, why is its conductivity different?
questions.learning_objective: Understand how the mobility of ions determines electrical conductivity in ionic compounds.
questions.target_misconception: The presence of charged particles is sufficient for a substance to conduct electricity, even if those particles cannot move.
solution_steps: Identify that solid salt contains positive and negative ions.
Explain that the ions are held in fixed positions in the solid crystal lattice.
Explain that electric current requires mobile charge carriers.
Describe how melting allows the ions to move.
Conclude that molten salt conducts because its ions are mobile.
questions.reference_answer: Solid salt contains ions, but they are fixed in the crystal lattice and cannot move freely to carry charge. When salt melts, the lattice breaks down and the ions become mobile. These moving ions carry electric current, so molten salt conducts electricity.

questions.question: A student adds water to a sample of a strong acid. Does the acid become more acidic or less acidic after dilution? What happens to its pH?
questions.learning_objective: Understand how dilution affects hydrogen ion concentration and pH.
questions.target_misconception: Adding water to an acid makes it more acidic because the volume of acidic solution increases.
solution_steps: Recall that pH depends on hydrogen ion concentration.
Explain that adding water increases the solution volume without adding more acid.
Recognize that the hydrogen ion concentration decreases.
Connect the lower hydrogen ion concentration to an increase in pH.
Clarify that the solution remains acidic after ordinary dilution, although it is less acidic.
questions.reference_answer: Adding water dilutes the acid and decreases its hydrogen ion concentration. Since pH = -log10[H+], the pH increases. The solution becomes less acidic, although it generally remains acidic after dilution.

questions.question: Consider the statement: 'If it rains, the roads become wet.' The roads are wet, so someone concludes that it must have rained. Is that conclusion logically guaranteed?
questions.learning_objective: Understand conditional statements and distinguish a valid inference from affirming the consequent.
questions.target_misconception: If P implies Q and Q is true, P must also be true.
solution_steps: Represent the statement as P implies Q, where P is rain and Q is wet roads.
Identify that the observation establishes Q, not P.
Consider other possible causes of wet roads, such as a sprinkler or cleaning.
Explain that P implies Q does not mean Q implies P.
Identify the inference as affirming the consequent and conclude that rain is not guaranteed.
questions.reference_answer: No. The original statement says rain is sufficient for wet roads, but it does not say rain is the only possible cause. The roads could be wet because of a sprinkler or another source. Concluding that it rained from the fact that the roads are wet is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

questions.subtopic: Boolean Logic and De Morgan's Laws
questions.question: A program checks whether both conditions A and B are true using A AND B. What should the program check to determine that this combined condition is NOT true: NOT A AND NOT B, or NOT A OR NOT B? Explain.
questions.learning_objective: Understand the negation of compound Boolean expressions using De Morgan's laws.
questions.target_misconception: Negating A AND B means negating both operands and keeping AND between them.
solution_steps: Interpret A AND B as true only when both A and B are true.
Ask when the combined condition is false: when at least one of A or B is false.
Represent that condition as NOT A OR NOT B.
Optionally verify the equivalence using a truth table.
State De Morgan's law: NOT (A AND B) equals (NOT A) OR (NOT B).
questions.reference_answer: The correct expression is NOT A OR NOT B. A AND B is false whenever at least one of the two conditions is false. De Morgan's law states that NOT (A AND B) is equivalent to (NOT A) OR (NOT B).

questions.question: A student claims that an algorithm with two nested loops must always have O(n^2) time complexity. Is this statement correct?
questions.learning_objective: Understand how loop execution counts determine asymptotic time complexity.
questions.target_misconception: Nested loops always imply quadratic complexity.
solution_steps: Clarify that the number of loop iterations determines complexity.
Consider an example where both loops execute n times.
Calculate the total operations as n times n.
Consider a nested loop where the inner loop executes a constant number of times.
Explain why nesting alone does not determine complexity.
questions.reference_answer: No. Two nested loops do not necessarily imply O(n^2). If both loops execute n times, the complexity is O(n^2). However, if the inner loop executes a constant number of times, the complexity may be O(n). The iteration bounds determine the complexity.

questions.question: Why can a program use a virtual memory address that is not currently mapped to a physical memory page and still execute successfully after accessing it?
questions.learning_objective: Understand virtual addressing, page tables and page faults.
questions.target_misconception: Every valid virtual memory address must always have a physical memory page loaded in RAM.
solution_steps: Distinguish virtual addresses from physical addresses.
Explain that page tables describe the mappings from virtual pages to physical frames.
Explain that a valid virtual page need not currently be resident in RAM.
Describe how accessing a non-resident valid page can trigger a page fault.
Explain that the operating system can load the page and update the mapping before execution resumes.
Distinguish a valid non-resident page from an invalid memory access.
questions.reference_answer: A process uses virtual addresses, which are translated through page tables by the memory management unit. A valid page may not currently be resident in RAM. Accessing it can trigger a page fault; the operating system can load the page from secondary storage, update the page table and resume the process. An invalid access may instead cause a protection error or segmentation fault.

questions.question: Why does binary search require the input array to be sorted? What could go wrong if we apply the usual binary-search procedure to an unsorted array?
questions.learning_objective: Understand the ordering property that makes binary search work.
questions.target_misconception: Binary search works on any array because it repeatedly checks the middle element.
solution_steps: Explain that binary search compares the target with the middle element.
Describe how the comparison determines which half can be discarded.
Connect that decision to the sorted order of the array.
Explain that an unsorted array provides no guarantee that the target is in the chosen half.
Conclude that the usual binary-search procedure may incorrectly discard the target.
questions.reference_answer: Binary search relies on sorted order. When the target is compared with the middle element, the ordering tells us whether the target can only be in the left or right half. In an unsorted array, that inference is invalid, so the algorithm may discard the half containing the target and return an incorrect result.

questions.question: A recursive function calls itself with a smaller input each time, but it has no base case. What is likely to happen when the function runs, and why is a base case necessary?
questions.learning_objective: Understand how base cases terminate recursive calls.
questions.target_misconception: Making the input smaller is sufficient for recursion to stop, even without an explicit terminating condition.
solution_steps: Recognize that each recursive call creates another pending function call.
Explain that a base case provides a condition under which no further recursive call is made.
Consider what happens when no such condition exists.
Explain that calls may continue until a resource limit, such as the call-stack limit, is reached.
Conclude that a correct recursive function needs a reachable base case and progress towards it.
questions.reference_answer: Without a base case, the function has no defined condition for stopping its recursive calls. It may keep calling itself until the program runs out of call-stack space and fails. A base case terminates recursion, while each recursive step should make progress towards reaching that case.

questions.question: A browser's Back operation needs to return to the most recently visited page first. Why is a stack a natural choice for implementing this behaviour rather than a queue?
questions.learning_objective: Understand the LIFO and FIFO access patterns of stacks and queues.
questions.target_misconception: A stack and a queue differ only in implementation, not in the order in which elements are removed.
solution_steps: Identify that the most recently visited page should be retrieved first.
Recall that a stack follows last-in, first-out order.
Recall that a queue follows first-in, first-out order.
Relate stack push and pop operations to browser navigation history.
Conclude that a stack matches the required access pattern more naturally.
questions.reference_answer: A stack follows LIFO: the last page added is the first page retrieved. This matches the Back operation, which returns to the most recently visited page. A queue follows FIFO and would retrieve the oldest stored page first, which does not match that behaviour.

questions.question: Suppose a Students table has a unique student_id, and an Enrollments table stores student_id to indicate which student took each course. Why should student_id be a primary key in Students and a foreign key in Enrollments?
questions.learning_objective: Understand entity identification and referential integrity in relational databases.
questions.target_misconception: A primary key and a foreign key are interchangeable because both contain identifiers.
solution_steps: Identify that each student row needs a unique identifier.
Explain that the Students.student_id primary key uniquely identifies a student.
Explain that Enrollments.student_id refers to a student in the Students table.
Describe how the foreign-key constraint helps prevent references to non-existent students.
Distinguish the identifying role of the primary key from the referencing role of the foreign key.
questions.reference_answer: Students.student_id is a primary key because it uniquely identifies each student row. Enrollments.student_id is a foreign key because it refers to that primary key and links each enrollment to an existing student. The foreign-key constraint helps maintain referential integrity.
